title: Requirements and the systems lifecycle
summary: A Claude app starts as a business problem. Turn it into functional requirements (what the app must do), derive the infrastructure requirements they imply, and record each decision with its context and trade-offs so it can be defended. Then carry the app through a lifecycle that loops: Requirements, Design, Build, Test, Deploy, Operate, Iterate.
keyPoints: **Functional** requirements decide whether the app performs its task; **nonfunctional** ones (latency, availability, scalability) decide how well. Both shape the design.
Outline an ideal interaction, then break it into every task Claude must perform, so each task can be prompted and evaluated.
Each function implies infrastructure: **real-time** data such as an account balance needs a lookup tool, because embedding-based RAG is not sufficient for it.
Justify every design decision with a business requirement, and record it in an **ADR**: context, options considered, decision, trade-offs, status.
Requirements become test cases. Defining eval tasks stress-tests whether requirements are concrete enough to start building.
The lifecycle is a loop: ship in short, gated releases, and let what Operate reveals feed the next cycle’s requirements.

sections.heading: From business problem to functional requirements
sections.body:
A business problem is not yet something you can build or test. The first step is to say what the app must do. Microsoft's architecture guidance draws the line this way:

- **Functional requirements** determine whether the application performs its task.
- **Nonfunctional requirements** determine how well it performs, such as its scalability, availability and latency.

Anthropic's customer support guide shows how to reach functional requirements. First outline an ideal customer interaction: how and when the customer interacts with Claude, and how Claude should respond. That outline helps determine the technical requirements of your solution. Then break the interaction into every task you want Claude to perform, such as greeting, answering product questions, staying on topic and generating a quote. Listing the tasks ensures you can prompt and evaluate Claude for every one, and shows the range of interactions your test cases must cover.

If the app automates work people already do, study how they do it today, as the ticket-routing guide advises: which rules exist, where they fail, and how edge cases are handled.
sections.example: Business problem: "Our agents spend too long on car-insurance questions and quotes." Ideal interaction: greet, answer questions about electric-vehicle coverage, steer off-topic questions back, ask the questions a quote needs, call the quote API, present the quote. Functional requirements, one per task: answer coverage questions from the insurer's own information; redirect off-topic questions; collect quote details and submit them to the quote API; present the result. Each line is now something to prompt for and write test cases against.

sections.heading: Deriving infrastructure requirements
sections.body:
Each functional requirement carries infrastructure with it. Anthropic's support guide gives two cases:

- Product information Claude must know has to be in its context, which might imply a RAG integration. With large amounts of context, putting everything in the prompt can mean high costs, slower responses and context-window limits.
- Real-time information, such as account balances or policy details, can't come from embedding-based RAG. It needs tool use, which brings live data into Claude's response.

The systems you connect to shape the design too. For ticket routing, a push-based integration (the ticketing system calls your service through a webhook) is more web-scalable but needs a public endpoint. A pull-based one (your code fetches tickets on a schedule) is easier, but polling too often makes unnecessary calls and polling too rarely makes routing slow. The choice depends on what APIs the ticketing system provides.

Nonfunctional targets come from the business, and they can differ per flow: different user, data or system flows often have different requirements for availability and scalability. Compliance can add more, such as controlling where inference runs and where data is stored at rest (data residency).
sections.example: A bank's assistant must "tell signed-in customers their current balance." That requirement implies a tool Claude can call to read the live balance from the bank's account system. A nightly embedding index of account data would not meet it, however good the retrieval, because embedding-based RAG is not sufficient for real-time information. A second requirement, "answer questions about our savings products", implies something different: product information in Claude's context, which might mean a RAG integration.

diagram.caption: Each layer is derived from the one before it.

steps.label: Infrastructure requirements
steps.sublabel: what it runs on and connects to

sections.heading: Documenting requirements so a decision can be defended
sections.body:
Every design decision must be justified by a business requirement. Objectives such as recovery time and acceptable outage should inform the architecture: if the business can tolerate a longer outage, adding redundancy might add cost for no business benefit.

Write requirements so results can be judged against them. Success criteria should be specific and measurable, and an evaluation needs clear thresholds, such as a target accuracy and a cost reduction against the current method. With thresholds set, you can tell with impartial empiricism which approach is best.

Then record the decision. An architecture decision record (ADR) documents key decisions, including the alternatives you ruled out. Each record holds:

- The problem statement and its context
- The options considered
- The decision, with its important trade-offs and confidence level
- A status, such as Proposed, Accepted or Superseded

Always include the rationale: without it, stakeholders can't tell whether a decision still applies when circumstances change. The log is append-only. If a decision changes, write a new record that supersedes the old one and link the two. Keep records short, and link longer design material instead of turning a record into a design guide.
sections.example: ADR-007, Accepted. Context: tickets must be routed within moments at high volume, for less per ticket than the current rules engine. Options: Claude Haiku 5.5, Claude Opus 5.5, keep the rules engine. Decision: Haiku 5.5 at low effort. Trade-off: less headroom for deep reasoning, accepted because routing is a simple, high-volume classification. Confidence: medium. Evidence: the eval met the agreed accuracy and cost thresholds. If categories later multiply and accuracy falls, a new record supersedes this one, and both stay in the log.

sections.heading: The lifecycle, phase by phase
sections.body:
NIST defines a system development life cycle as the scope of activities for a system, from initiation through development and acquisition, implementation, operation and maintenance, to its eventual disposal. Applied to a Claude application, the course names seven phases:

- **Requirements:** functional and infrastructure requirements, with success criteria and ways to test them.
- **Design:** components, integrations and model choice. Find the simplest solution possible and add complexity only when needed.
- **Build:** prompts, tools and the service around them.
- **Test:** evals against the success criteria. Early on, product requirements naturally translate into test cases.
- **Deploy:** move changes through stages to production, with gates and approvals.
- **Operate:** monitor, maintain and troubleshoot in production, including tracking model deprecations.
- **Iterate:** feed what you learn back into the requirements.

The order matters. Anthropic's prompt engineering overview assumes the first phase is done before prompt work starts: a clear definition of success criteria, some ways to empirically test against them, and a first draft prompt. If they're missing, establish them first.
sections.example: A claims-intake assistant through the loop. Requirements: extract the policy number and incident date, reply within seconds, meet the agreed accuracy threshold. Design: a fixed extraction workflow with one lookup tool, not an autonomous agent. Build: the prompt, the tool and an API service. Test: an eval set of real emails, edge cases included. Deploy: through staging, with an approval gate. Operate: telemetry, alerts and a watch on the model's deprecation status. Iterate: a new claim type appears in production, so it becomes a new requirement and new test cases.

diagram.caption: Seven phases, and Iterate leads back to Requirements.

sections.heading: Test, deploy and operate: closing the loop
sections.body:
Build evals early. Anthropic's evals post says they are especially useful at the start of development to explicitly encode expected behavior: two engineers reading the same initial spec can come away with different interpretations, and an eval suite resolves this. Defining eval tasks is one of the best ways to stress-test whether requirements are concrete enough to start building. Evals get harder to build the longer you wait; wait too long and you're reverse-engineering success criteria from a live system.

Deploy in small steps. DevOps guidance favors shorter release cycles, because incremental progress makes planning and risk management easier and reduces the impact on stability. Delivery uses a release management process with clear manual approval stages, and automated gates between stages.

Operate with visibility. Continuous monitoring collects telemetry and sets alerts, and its insights help the team see how to improve the application in future development cycles. Models have a lifecycle too: once a model is deprecated, migrate all usage before the retirement date, and test with the replacement well before it.

Then iterate. A gap that monitoring reveals is a requirements gap, so it goes back to the start of the loop.
sections.example: Three months after launch, alerts show a growing share of chats about a new product line, and the bot handles them poorly. The team doesn't patch the production prompt on the spot. They add the product line to the requirements, write eval tasks for it, change the prompt and the retrieved content, run the evals and ship through the same gated release. Later, the model the app uses is deprecated; the same eval suite tests the replacement well before the retirement date.
